claims.text: Controlled nitrogen doping of the multi-element alloy catalyst can induce metal–nitrogen bonds.
Annealing in an NH3 atmosphere can selectively incorporate nitrogen into the catalyst surface layers.
The resulting surface metal–nitrogen bonds will be robust under the proposed operating conditions.
Metal–nitrogen bonds alter the alloy's local electronic or core structure.
Nitrogen incorporation and metal–nitrogen bonding stabilize catalytically active sites.
Metal–nitrogen bonding can enhance catalyst activity and durability through a structural distortion effect.
Nitrogen doping will reduce leaching of less-noble metals from the catalyst.
Nitrogen doping will inhibit degradation caused by corrosive gasoline-exhaust species, including H2O and NO.
Nitrogen doping will inhibit degradation caused by thermal cycling and automotive thermal aging.
Preservation of active sites by nitrogen doping can compensate for low platinum-group-metal content.
The nitrogen-doped catalyst will have a lower degradation rate than the untreated catalyst under transient low-temperature exhaust conditions.
The nitrogen-doped catalyst will sustain higher CO conversion than the untreated catalyst.
The nitrogen-doped catalyst will sustain higher NO conversion or reduction efficiency than the untreated catalyst.
The nitrogen-doped catalyst will show less metal leaching than the untreated catalyst.
The untreated starting catalyst suffers significant activity loss and durability limitations under comparable exhaust and aging conditions.
Insufficient nitrogen incorporation will fail to provide the proposed benefit.
Overly aggressive nitrogen-doping conditions may compromise intrinsic active sites.
The intervention is primarily applicable to moderate-temperature, transient gasoline or hybrid-vehicle exhaust operation.
A nitrogen-containing PtCoFeNiCu high-entropy-alloy electrocatalyst with multiple metal–nitrogen bonds has demonstrated high electrochemical durability and ORR performance with reduced Pt usage.
